plants.description: The cornerstone of eastern food webs. Supports more caterpillar species than any other local tree and feeds birds, mammals, and fungi.
A larval powerhouse with early nectar, summer fruit for birds, and high wildlife value in hedgerows and woodland edges.
A late-season nectar and pollen jackpot. Goldenrods support specialist bees, caterpillars, and migrating monarchs.
Fast-growing native shade tree with spring flowers, brilliant fall color, and strong caterpillar support.
A long-lived shade tree with glossy foliage, scarlet fall color, and small fruits that disappear quickly into migrating birds.
A fast-growing canopy tree with distinctive leaves and flowers. Best for larger yards with room for a 60-foot spread.
An understory tree with early nectar for bees and a compact form that fits small yards. Hosts several specialist moths.
A four-season native: early blossoms, June berries for birds, clean summer foliage, and orange-red fall color.
An understory beauty that feeds pollinators, birds, and caterpillars. Best with afternoon shade and consistent moisture.
Evergreen structure and winter berries for birds. Plant a male nearby for reliable fruit on female selections.
A tough evergreen that shelters birds in winter and provides dense cover. Great for windy or dry edges.
A native evergreen shrub with spring nectar and year-round cover. Keep it mulched and protected from afternoon sun.
A native evergreen screen that provides nesting and winter cover. Better than most exotic hedges for local birds.
A deciduous holly that lights up winter with red fruit for robins and waxwings. Needs a male pollinator.
A productive native shrub for people and wildlife: spring nectar, summer berries, fall color, and strong caterpillar support.
A low, spreading blueberry for sunny edges. Adds nectar, fruit, and caterpillar habitat without needing a big footprint.
A tough, low shrub with glossy leaves, red fall color, and berry-like fruit for birds. Excellent on slopes and dry edges.
A durable native shrub with peeling bark, pollinator-friendly flowers, and excellent erosion control.
A bird-friendly shrub with spring flowers, blue-black fruit, and dense cover. A strong replacement for exotic hedges.
An early-season woodland shrub and host for spicebush swallowtails. Plant a male and female for red fall berries.
Fragrant summer flowers feed bees and butterflies when little else is blooming. Tolerates wet soils and shade.
A native hydrangea with oak-shaped leaves, long-lasting blooms, and burgundy fall color. More ecological value than mophead hydrangeas.
A fast evergreen screen for coastal and warm-edge gardens. Provides cover and waxy berries for birds.
A native evergreen holly that makes a dense, low-maintenance hedge and supports pollinators and birds.
A vigorous native groundcover for shade. Evergreen foliage suppresses weeds and early flowers feed newly emerged bees.
A low woodland groundcover with heart-shaped leaves and hidden flowers. Spreads slowly to form a weed-resistant carpet.
A cheerful native groundcover for shade edges. Blooms over a long season and slowly knits the garden floor together.
A soft, lawn-like native sedge for dry shade. A low-input alternative to turfgrass under trees.
A sturdy native grass with airy seed heads, winter structure, and bird cover. Replaces invasive reed canary grass and miscanthus.
A drought-tough native grass with blue-green summer foliage and copper fall color. Excellent for sunny, low-water borders.
A long-blooming native perennial with nectar and seed for wildlife. A direct replacement for daylily mass plantings.
A woodland perennial with early nectar and caterpillar support. Forms a tidy clump and tolerates dry shade once established.
A sculptural native fern for moist shade. Provides cover for amphibians and insects and replaces hosta clumps gracefully.
A graceful, easy fern for shade gardens. Its fine texture pairs well with foamflower and wild ginger.
A native shade perennial with foamy spring flowers and semi-evergreen foliage. Spreads gently into a groundcover.
A native coralbell with mottled evergreen leaves and tiny pollinator-friendly flowers. Tough in dry shade.
A late-summer blue flower for wet spots. Feeds bumblebees and hummingbirds and replaces purple loosestrife in rain gardens.
A vigorous native vine with blue berries for birds and scarlet fall color. Use it where it has room to roam, not on fragile structures.
A well-behaved native vine with tubular flowers for hummingbirds. Far better than invasive Japanese honeysuckle.
A restrained native wisteria that flowers on new wood and supports pollinators. Still needs a strong trellis.
A native rose with single pink flowers, rose hips for birds, and none of the thuggish spread of multiflora rose.
A native iris for rain gardens and wet edges. Provides early nectar and replaces invasive yellow flag iris.
A pollinator favorite with long bloom and seed for finches. Drought-tolerant once established.
A monarch host plant with brilliant orange flowers. Needs well-drained soil and room for its taproot.
A mint-family native that feeds long-tongued bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds. Mildew-resistant with good airflow.
A late-season nectar source that keeps pollinators fed into frost. Pinch in early summer for a compact habit.
A tall, architectural native that draws butterflies and native bees. Ideal for rain gardens and wet back borders.
An early-season umbel that supports short-tongued bees and serves as a host for black swallowtails.
A beautiful but non-native understory tree. It offers little caterpillar food compared with serviceberry or dogwood.
A shade-garden staple from East Asia. It is not invasive in most gardens, but it replaces native groundcover that supports insects.
A popular ornamental with showy mophead flowers. Native oakleaf hydrangea and summersweet offer more pollinator value.
A clipped evergreen hedge from Europe. It provides structure but little food; native inkberry and wax myrtle do both.
A beloved old-fashioned ornamental. Keep it if you love it, but pair it with native perennials that carry the food web.
A drought-tolerant Mediterranean plant that feeds some generalist bees. Not a substitute for regionally native nectar plants.
A tough edging plant from East Asia. Native sedge and green-and-gold provide similar texture with more ecological value.
An early spring bulb that is not invasive. Enjoy it, but add native spring ephemerals for early pollinators.
A classic spring bulb with limited value for local pollinators. Treat as seasonal color, not habitat.
A dense, shade-casting tree that seeds prolifically into woodlands. Its roots and leaf litter suppress native understory plants.
Bird-dispersed berries move this shrub into forests, where dense thickets crowd out native regeneration. Its fall color is not worth the ecological cost.
A thorny shrub that spreads by seed and root fragments. Dense thickets alter soil chemistry and create tick-friendly habitat.
A smothering vine that climbs trees, weighs down limbs, and creates a monoculture on the forest floor. It also harbors pests and disease.
A tough spreader that forms dense tuber mats and escapes into roadsides and woodland edges. Often confused with native lilies.
A shade groundcover that forms dense mats and spreads into forests. It suppresses native spring ephemerals and tree seedlings.
A bird-dispersed shrub that forms dense thickets in forests and edges. Its spring flowers are mostly ignored by native specialists.
A fast vine that smothers shrubs and small trees. It spreads by runners and bird-dispersed fruit and is a major forest threat.
A vigorous vine that girdles trees and spreads by runners. Its spectacular flowers hide a serious woodland impact.
A aggressive vine that strangles trees and hybridizes with native bittersweet. Its orange berries are spread by birds.
A thorny shrub that forms impenetrable thickets in pastures and woodland edges. It spreads by seed and rooting stems.
A wetland invader that forms dense stands and displaces native marsh plants. It produces millions of seeds and spreads by fragments.
A tall wetland grass that forms monocultures, alters hydrology, and displaces native marsh habitat. A serious restoration challenge.
An annual grass that carpets forest floors and lawns, outcompeting native seedlings. It spreads by tiny seeds on shoes, tires, and water.
A shade invader that releases chemicals that suppress native plants and mycorrhizal fungi. It spreads rapidly by seed.
A fast-growing tree that spreads by seed and root suckers. It is the preferred host of spotted lanternfly and damages pavement and foundations.
A nitrogen-fixing shrub that alters soil and outcompetes native plants. Its abundant red berries are spread widely by birds.
An evergreen vine and groundcover that smothers native plants and climbs trees. It spreads by rooting stems and bird-dispersed seed.
A wetland iris that spreads by rhizomes and seeds, forming dense stands that displace native marsh vegetation.
A fast-growing vine that blankets trees, buildings, and roadsides. Eradication usually requires a multi-year professional plan.
A shrub or small tree that spreads into forests and alters soil. Its berries are laxative to birds and its dense shade suppresses regeneration.
A popular ornamental that spreads by seed and root suckers. Its berries can be toxic to pets and birds, and it invades forests in warmer regions.
An evergreen shrub that spreads by bird-dispersed seed into forests. It can form dense understories that crowd out native plants.
A brittle ornamental tree that spreads into roadsides and old fields. Its early flowers offer little to native pollinators, and its structure fails in storms.
A fast-growing tree that hybridizes with native red mulberry and spreads into forests. Its pollen is a common allergen.
A fast-growing tree that spreads by seed into disturbed areas and outcompetes native trees. It is brittle and short-lived.
A popular ornamental grass that seeds into meadows and roadsides, forming dense stands that crowd out native warm-season grasses.
An early yellow-flowered shrub with little caterpillar value. Northern spicebush offers the same early-season yellow glow and hosts the spicebush swallowtail.
A shade-tolerant evergreen groundcover that forms a sterile carpet. Native golden ragwort and green-and-gold support early pollinators instead.
A shade-tolerant shrub that leafs out early and holds leaves late, suppressing native understory plants and spreading bird-dispersed fruit.
A low, fast-spreading native groundcover with spring flowers and small edible fruit. It supports early bees and birds.
A compact native shrub with frothy white flowers that feed bees and beneficial insects. It is a strong replacement for barberry in sunny beds.
A native hydrangea with white flower clusters and good shade tolerance. It offers more pollinator value than bigleaf hydrangea.
A clump-forming goldenrod with showy plumes that feed late-season bees, butterflies, and migrating monarchs.
A pollinator magnet with silvery bracts and a long bloom window. It is deer-resistant and tolerates average to moist soil.

removalProtocols.method: Cut the tree low and treat the stump immediately with a targeted cut-stump herbicide applied by a licensed professional. For small saplings, hand-pull after rain.
removalProtocols.timing: Late summer to early fall, when the tree is moving sugars to its roots. Avoid spring sap flow.
removalProtocols.safety: Wear eye protection and gloves. Do not use herbicide near waterways or on windy days. Follow the label exactly.
removalProtocols.disposal: Bag seed-bearing branches and send to municipal yard waste. Do not compost viable seeds.

removalProtocols.method: Cut-stump or root-wrench small plants. For larger shrubs, cut stems and treat the cambium ring with a targeted herbicide. Revisit for root sprouts.
removalProtocols.timing: Late summer through fall. Remove before berries ripen to prevent bird dispersal.
removalProtocols.safety: Bag berries and stems. Wear gloves; the sap can irritate skin. Avoid herbicide near desirable plants.
removalProtocols.disposal: Double-bag fruit-bearing material and send to landfill or municipal yard waste. Never dump in a woodland.

removalProtocols.method: Use a root wrench or mattock to remove the crown and major roots. For large infestations, cut and treat the stump; monitor for resprouts.
removalProtocols.timing: Early spring before fruit set or fall after seed dispersal. Remove fruit-bearing stems first.
removalProtocols.safety: Wear heavy gloves and eye protection. Avoid disturbing soil more than necessary to limit seed germination.
removalProtocols.disposal: Bag all root crowns and fruit. Do not compost; root fragments can resprout.

removalProtocols.method: Cut a 3-foot gap in every vine around the tree trunk, then hand-pull the ground mat after rain. Solarize dense patches with clear plastic for one growing season.
removalProtocols.timing: Late fall through early spring, when native wildlife is less active and soil is workable.
removalProtocols.safety: Do not pull ivy off a tree canopy; cut at the base and let it dry. Wear gloves and long sleeves.
removalProtocols.disposal: Bag vines and roots. Do not compost or leave piles on site—fragments can root.

removalProtocols.method: Dig the entire tuber mass with a garden fork. Sift the soil and remove every finger-like tuber; any fragment can regenerate.
removalProtocols.timing: Spring before flowering or late summer after bloom. Repeat for two seasons.
removalProtocols.safety: Lift with your legs and wear gloves. Mark the area so you can catch resprouts.
removalProtocols.disposal: Bag tubers and send to municipal yard waste. Do not compost.

removalProtocols.method: Hand-pull or rake out runners after rain. For dense mats, solarize or smother with cardboard and 3–4 inches of mulch for a full season.
removalProtocols.timing: Early spring before new growth or fall. Revisit monthly for resprouts.
removalProtocols.safety: Avoid burying desirable plants under cardboard. Keep plastic sheeting secure and remove it before summer heat.
removalProtocols.disposal: Bag runners and roots. Do not compost.

removalProtocols.method: Cut-stump treatment or repeated cutting. Pull seedlings by hand. Remove before berries ripen to reduce spread.
removalProtocols.timing: Late summer to fall. Follow up in spring for root sprouts.
removalProtocols.safety: Wear gloves and eye protection. Treat stumps immediately; privet resprouts vigorously.
removalProtocols.disposal: Bag fruit and roots. Do not compost.

removalProtocols.method: Cut vines at the base and unwind them from trunks. Pull runners by hand after rain. Repeat cutting every few weeks.
removalProtocols.timing: Spring through fall, before fruit ripens. Persistence matters more than a single pass.
removalProtocols.safety: Do not yank vines from tree canopies; cut and let them dry. Wear gloves.
removalProtocols.disposal: Bag vines and roots. Do not compost or leave on site.

removalProtocols.method: Cut all stems at ground level, then dig out the root crown and runners. Treat resprouts with a targeted cut-stump method.
removalProtocols.timing: Late summer to fall. Remove seed pods before they open.
removalProtocols.safety: Wear eye protection. Do not let vines pull down structures. Work with a partner for large crowns.
removalProtocols.disposal: Bag seed pods and roots. Do not compost.

removalProtocols.method: Cut vines at the base and remove the root crown. Pull seedlings. Revisit for resprouts and remove fruit before it ripens.
removalProtocols.timing: Late summer to fall. Cut before berries turn orange.
removalProtocols.safety: Do not pull vines from the canopy. Wear gloves and eye protection.
removalProtocols.disposal: Bag fruit and roots. Do not compost.

removalProtocols.method: Cut the crown and treat the stump, or use a root wrench for small plants. Repeated cutting weakens large stands.
removalProtocols.timing: Late summer to fall. Remove rose hips to reduce bird dispersal.
removalProtocols.safety: Wear heavy leather gloves and eye protection. Avoid herbicide near waterways.
removalProtocols.disposal: Bag roots and hips. Do not compost.

removalProtocols.method: Hand-pull small plants before seed set, removing the entire root. For large stands, cut flower spikes and use targeted aquatic-approved treatment with a professional.
removalProtocols.timing: Early summer before flowering, then again before seed set.
removalProtocols.safety: Do not use ordinary herbicides near water. Use only aquatic-approved products applied by a licensed professional.
removalProtocols.disposal: Bag flower spikes and roots. Do not compost or move fragments to other waterways.

removalProtocols.method: Small patches: cut repeatedly and smother. Large stands require a professional integrated plan with aquatic-approved treatment and native replanting.
removalProtocols.timing: Late summer to early fall, before seed dispersal. Coordinate with local land managers.
removalProtocols.safety: Do not attempt large-scale herbicide work yourself. Protect waterways and use permitted methods only.
removalProtocols.disposal: Bag seed heads. Do not move rhizomes to other sites.

removalProtocols.method: Hand-pull or mow before seed set in late summer. Repeat for 3–5 years to exhaust the seed bank. Clean boots and tools afterward.
removalProtocols.timing: Late summer before seed heads form. A second pass in early fall.
removalProtocols.safety: Avoid walking through seed heads. Clean gear before leaving the site.
removalProtocols.disposal: Bag pulled plants. Do not compost.

removalProtocols.method: Hand-pull before flowering, getting the taproot. For dense patches, cut flower stalks and bag them. Repeat for several years.
removalProtocols.timing: Early spring before seed set. Revisit in late spring for missed plants.
removalProtocols.safety: Wear gloves. Clean boots and tools to avoid spreading seed.
removalProtocols.disposal: Bag all flowering plants. Do not compost.

removalProtocols.method: Do not simply cut it—root suckers explode. Use a professional cut-stump or basal treatment plan, then remove suckers. For small seedlings, pull after rain.
removalProtocols.timing: Late summer to early fall, when roots are storing reserves.
removalProtocols.safety: This species needs a multi-year plan. Avoid cutting without treatment; it can make the infestation worse.
removalProtocols.disposal: Bag seed clusters. Do not move roots or soil containing root fragments.

removalProtocols.method: Cut-stump treatment or root-wrench small plants. Remove before fruit ripens. Expect resprouts and monitor for several years.
removalProtocols.timing: Late summer to fall, before berries are fully ripe.
removalProtocols.safety: Wear gloves and eye protection. Avoid disturbing soil; it stimulates seed germination.
removalProtocols.disposal: Bag fruit and roots. Do not compost.

removalProtocols.method: Cut vines at the base and pull the ground mat after rain. Solarize dense patches. Revisit for resprouts.
removalProtocols.timing: Late fall through early spring.
removalProtocols.safety: Do not pull from tree canopies. Wear gloves and long sleeves.
removalProtocols.disposal: Bag vines and roots. Do not compost.

removalProtocols.method: Dig the rhizome mass with a fork, removing all fragments. Cut seed pods before they open. Repeat for several years.
removalProtocols.timing: Late summer to early fall, after flowering but before seed release.
removalProtocols.safety: Wear gloves. Work carefully in wet soils and avoid spreading fragments downstream.
removalProtocols.disposal: Bag rhizomes and seed pods. Do not compost or dump near water.

removalProtocols.method: Do not attempt to dig large crowns alone. Cut vines and coordinate with a professional for repeated treatment and native replanting.
removalProtocols.timing: Late summer to fall. Remove before seed pods mature.
removalProtocols.safety: Wear protective clothing. Large infestations can hide hazards and should be handled by professionals.
removalProtocols.disposal: Bag roots and seed pods. Do not move plant material off-site.

removalProtocols.method: Cut-stump treatment for larger plants; hand-pull seedlings. Remove before fruit ripens. Monitor for resprouts.
removalProtocols.timing: Late summer to fall.
removalProtocols.safety: Wear gloves. Treat stumps immediately to prevent resprouting.
removalProtocols.disposal: Bag fruit and roots. Do not compost.

removalProtocols.method: Dig out the root crown and remove all suckers. Cut-stump treatment for large plants. Remove berry clusters before they ripen.
removalProtocols.timing: Late summer to fall.
removalProtocols.safety: Wear gloves. Keep berries away from pets and children.
removalProtocols.disposal: Bag berries and roots. Do not compost.

removalProtocols.method: Cut-stump treatment or dig out the root crown. Remove fruit before it ripens. Monitor for seedlings.
removalProtocols.timing: Late winter to early spring, before fruit set, or fall.
removalProtocols.safety: Wear gloves; the leaves are spiny.
removalProtocols.disposal: Bag fruit and roots. Do not compost.

removalProtocols.method: Cut-stump treatment or remove the entire root crown. Remove before fruit ripens. Monitor for suckers.
removalProtocols.timing: Late summer to fall.
removalProtocols.safety: Wear eye protection. Do not leave cut branches with fruit on site.
removalProtocols.disposal: Bag fruit. Do not compost.

removalProtocols.method: Cut-stump treatment or remove the root crown. Remove fruit before it ripens. Monitor for root suckers.
removalProtocols.timing: Late summer to fall.
removalProtocols.safety: Wear gloves; the milky sap can irritate skin.
removalProtocols.disposal: Bag fruit and roots. Do not compost.

removalProtocols.method: Cut-stump treatment or remove the root crown. Remove seed-bearing branches. Monitor for resprouts.
removalProtocols.timing: Late summer to fall.
removalProtocols.safety: Wear eye protection. Avoid working near utility lines.
removalProtocols.disposal: Bag seed-bearing material. Do not compost.

removalProtocols.method: Dig out the entire clump before seed heads mature. Remove the crown and root mass; bag seed-bearing stems.
removalProtocols.timing: Late summer before seed set, or early spring.
removalProtocols.safety: Wear gloves and eye protection. Avoid disturbing wet soils or steep banks.
removalProtocols.disposal: Bag seed heads and send to municipal yard waste. Do not compost.

removalProtocols.method: Cut and roll back the mat, then sheet-mulch or hand-pull resprouts. Replant immediately with a native groundcover to suppress reinvasion.
removalProtocols.timing: Spring or early fall while soil is workable.
removalProtocols.safety: Wear gloves. Work in sections and keep roots out of storm drains.
removalProtocols.disposal: Bag roots and stems. Do not compost or dump near woodlands.

removalProtocols.method: Cut-stump treatment or pull seedlings when soil is moist. Remove root crowns and bag fruit-bearing branches.
removalProtocols.timing: Late summer to early fall, before fruit ripens.
removalProtocols.safety: Wear gloves and eye protection. Treat cut stumps according to local guidance.
removalProtocols.disposal: Bag fruit and roots. Do not compost or leave cut stems on site.
